name: 80,000 Hours
tagline: Ranks 'extreme power concentration' among the top global problems
description: 80,000 Hours is an organization (founded 2011, Oxford) that researches the world's most pressing problems and advises people on high-impact careers. It elevated 'extreme power concentration' to one of its top-ranked problem areas, publishing a detailed problem profile arguing that advanced AI could let a small group seize unprecedented, durable control, even over democratic institutions: via automated military coups, AI systems with 'secret loyalties,' economic capture and epistemic manipulation. Its widely heard podcast has featured deep-dive episodes such as Tom Davidson on AI-enabled human power grabs. By framing power concentration as a tractable, high-priority cause, 80,000 Hours channels talent and attention toward AI's structural risks to democracy.
aiDemocracyAngle: Ranks 'extreme power concentration' among the top global problems and routes talent and public attention toward preventing AI-enabled coups and disempowerment.

name: ACS Research Group (Alignment of Complex Systems)
tagline: Prague academic lab that originated the 'gradual disempowerment' thesis
description: The Alignment of Complex Systems (ACS) Research Group is an academic AI-safety lab housed at the Center for Theoretical Study, Charles University in Prague, led by Jan Kulveit. It studies multi-agent systems composed of humans and advanced AI, drawing on machine learning, information theory, active inference, network theory and ecology to understand how AI interacts with people and institutions and how to keep those interactions aligned with shared human values like freedom, kindness and justice. ACS is the intellectual home of the 'Gradual Disempowerment' thesis, which argues that incremental AI progress can erode human influence over the economy, culture and states without any dramatic takeover. Its researchers also work on hierarchical agency, cooperative AI and multi-agent risk. Funding comes from the Center for Theoretical Study and the Czech nonprofit Epistea. The group publishes academic papers, mentors researchers, and collaborates with Telic Research, the AI Objectives Institute and academics at Montreal and Toronto.
aiDemocracyAngle: Originated the 'gradual disempowerment' framing: AI can quietly displace humans from the economic, cultural and political systems democracy depends on, even absent a coup or rogue AI.

keyProjects.name: Gradual Disempowerment
keyProjects.note: Flagship 2025 paper on systemic existential risk

name: Ada Lovelace Institute
tagline: Making data and AI work for people and society
description: The Ada Lovelace Institute is an independent research institute and deliberative body based in the UK, established in 2018 by the Nuffield Foundation (with partners including the Alan Turing Institute and the Royal Society). Its mission is to ensure data and AI work for people and society. A distinctive strand of its work is democratic and participatory AI governance: it researches public attitudes to AI, runs citizens' juries and deliberative panels, and studies how to involve affected communities in decisions about AI. Its Going Public and People's Panel on AI projects demonstrate deliberative mechanisms, including a sortition-selected public panel that reviewed AI at low cost, and it examines public participation inside commercial AI labs. Ada combines this with policy research on AI regulation, biometrics and health data, feeding recommendations to UK and EU policymakers.
aiDemocracyAngle: Pioneers deliberative and participatory methods so the public, not just companies and governments, shapes how AI is built and regulated.

name: AI & Democracy Foundation
tagline: Governance innovation lab making democratic systems fit for a world with AI
description: The AI & Democracy Foundation (AIDF) is a nonprofit governance innovation organization founded in 2024 by Aviv Ovadya, operating as Thoughtful Tech Project Inc, a California 501(c)(3). It works so that trustworthy democratic processes, especially representative deliberations like citizens' assemblies, are available and empowered for decisions about AI. Its work runs along three tracks: strategy (the Democracy Levels framework, accepted at ICML 2025, and a Democratic Capabilities Gap Map at democracy.build), capacity-building (the DelibTech Network with DemocracyNext, facilitation training with FIDE, a Deliberative Tools Access Program) and adoption with AI companies, governments and funders. Ovadya previously advised OpenAI's Democratic Inputs to AI program and Meta on deliberative governance.
aiDemocracyAngle: Builds the frameworks, tools ecosystem and practitioner networks needed for deliberative democratic processes to actually govern AI, as an alternative to concentrated corporate or state control.

name: The AI Democracy Projects
tagline: Testing how AI systems perform on elections and democracy
description: The AI Democracy Projects are a collaboration between Proof News, the nonprofit investigative newsroom founded by journalist Julia Angwin, and the Science, Technology, and Social Values Lab at the Institute for Advanced Study (led by former OSTP director Alondra Nelson). The initiative runs domain-specific AI safety testing to measure how leading models answer questions real voters ask. In a January 2024 pilot, more than 40 election officials and AI experts rated 130 responses from Claude, Gemini, GPT-4, Llama 2 and Mixtral for bias, accuracy, completeness and harmfulness, finding many answers inaccurate or misleading. Follow-up studies documented worse performance in Spanish than English, gaps between companies' election-safety promises and behavior, and weak consent checks in AI voice-cloning services. Findings are published as open journalism and datasets for other researchers to build on.
aiDemocracyAngle: Empirically tests whether mainstream AI chatbots give voters accurate election information, holding model builders publicly accountable.

name: AI Futures Project
tagline: Forecasting group behind the 'AI 2027' loss-of-control scenario
description: The AI Futures Project is a Berkeley-based nonprofit research group forecasting the trajectory and societal impact of advanced AI, founded by former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo with a team including Eli Lifland, Thomas Larsen and Romeo Dean. It is best known for 'AI 2027,' a detailed month-by-month scenario of how a hard takeoff could unfold. One branch has competitive and bureaucratic pressures leading humans to lose meaningful control over increasingly autonomous AI, with power concentrating in whoever commands the leading models. The group builds quantitative timelines and forecasting models (for example, for automated AI R&D) and uses concrete scenarios to make abstract risks legible to policymakers and the public. Funded by charitable donations and grants, it publishes scenarios, forecasts and commentary aimed at improving strategic preparation for transformative AI.
aiDemocracyAngle: AI 2027 dramatizes loss-of-control and power-concentration pathways, showing how race dynamics could funnel decisive power to a handful of actors or to the AI systems themselves.

name: AI Now Institute
tagline: Confronting the concentration of power in the AI industry
description: The AI Now Institute is a US research and policy institute founded in 2017 by Kate Crawford and Meredith Whittaker to study the social implications of artificial intelligence. Now led by Amba Kak and Sarah Myers West, it focuses on the concentration of economic and political power in a handful of AI firms and develops policy strategies to redirect AI away from unchecked commercial surveillance and toward public accountability. Its annual Landscape Reports, such as 2025's Artificial Power, argue that a few companies controlling data, compute and infrastructure gain outsized influence over democratic institutions, and it publishes work on Power and Governance in the Age of AI. AI Now advises regulators and lawmakers in the US and EU on antitrust, worker power and structural approaches to AI governance. It frames the balance of power between AI companies and the public as a defining democratic question of the decade.
aiDemocracyAngle: Frames concentrated corporate control of AI as a threat to democracy and pushes structural policy (antitrust, accountability) to rebalance power toward the public.

keyProjects.note: Policy framing of AI and democracy

name: AI Objectives Institute (AOI)
tagline: Directing AI and economic systems toward human autonomy and flourishing
description: The AI Objectives Institute (AOI) is a nonprofit research lab founded in 2021 by the late internet-freedom pioneer Peter Eckersley. It works to ensure that large-scale systems (AI, markets and bureaucracies) are built and deployed around genuine human objectives, enabled by broad public input and scalable cooperation. Its research spans sociotechnical alignment (favoring governable institutions and AI), scalable coordination (making deliberation and cooperation work at scale) and human autonomy. AOI's flagship tool, Talk to the City, is an open-source LLM interface that analyzes large volumes of qualitative public input, such as interviews and survey responses, to surface collective viewpoints for deliberation and decision-making, used in citizen-assembly and civic contexts. Other work includes the AI Supply Chain Observatory. By turning collective input into legible signal, AOI aims to strengthen democratic agency in an AI-shaped economy rather than concentrate power.
aiDemocracyAngle: Develops open tools like Talk to the City that let large groups deliberate and feed collective views into decisions, boosting democratic agency.

name: AlgorithmWatch
tagline: So algorithms and AI strengthen rather than weaken democracy
description: AlgorithmWatch is a nonprofit research and advocacy organization based in Berlin and Zurich, founded in 2017. It evaluates the social impact of automated decision-making (ADM) and AI systems, fighting for a world where these technologies strengthen justice, human rights, democracy and sustainability rather than undermine them. Its work combines investigative research, public-interest journalism and policy advocacy on transparency, oversight and accountability. Democracy-focused projects examine how social-media recommender systems shape political debate and elections, including data-donation studies of platform algorithms during European votes, and push for enforceable transparency and researcher data access under the EU's Digital Services Act. It runs an Algorithmic Accountability Reporting Fellowship supporting journalists investigating automation in sensitive domains, and publishes policy positions to EU and national lawmakers. A Swiss sister organization, AlgorithmWatch CH, extends the work in Switzerland.
aiDemocracyAngle: Investigates how platform algorithms and public-sector AI shape elections and public discourse, pressing for transparency and democratic oversight.

name: Alliance for Securing Democracy (German Marshall Fund)
tagline: GMF initiative exposing authoritarian information manipulation via the Hamilton dashboard
description: The Alliance for Securing Democracy (ASD), a nonpartisan initiative housed at the German Marshall Fund of the United States since 2017, exposes and counters foreign authoritarian interference in democratic processes from Russia, China, and Iran. Its signature technology tool is the Hamilton 2.0 dashboard, which uses natural language processing, machine learning, and automated translation to categorize narratives and topics pushed by Russian, Chinese, and Iranian state officials and state media across X, Telegram, YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and state news sites. ASD also runs the Authoritarian Interference Tracker and an Information Manipulation workstream, and its broader analysis increasingly covers AI-enabled influence operations and emerging technology threats to democracy. ASD merged into the Institute for Strategic Dialogue (US) effective January 1, 2026; securingdemocracy.org is maintained as a community resource and archive.
aiDemocracyAngle: The Hamilton 2.0 dashboard applies NLP and machine learning to surface state-backed information manipulation, tracking how authoritarian actors weaponize the information space against democracies.

name: Alliance of Democracies Foundation
tagline: Rasmussen's foundation; its Transatlantic Commission on Election Integrity tackled deepfakes
description: Founded in 2017 by former NATO Secretary General Anders Fogh Rasmussen, the Alliance of Democracies Foundation is a Copenhagen-based nonprofit that advances democracy globally and convenes the annual Copenhagen Democracy Summit. Its technology workstream was the Transatlantic Commission on Election Integrity (TCEI), launched in 2018 with Michael Chertoff and other transatlantic leaders to counter foreign election interference. TCEI has focused on deepfakes and AI-generated disinformation: examining how synthetic video and audio threaten democracies, developing technology tools (an early demonstration used AI firm ASI Data Science), and promoting the Pledge for Election Integrity for candidates and parties. The commission now appears inactive.
aiDemocracyAngle: The Transatlantic Commission on Election Integrity was among the first to spotlight AI deepfakes as an election threat, building tools and pledges to counter synthetic-media disinformation.

name: Alliance4Europe
tagline: Pan-European network coordinating defense against information manipulation
description: Alliance4Europe is a European civil-society organization that strengthens democracy by countering disinformation and foreign information manipulation. Its flagship, the Counter Disinformation Network (CDN), is a collaboration and crisis-response platform bringing together over 440 in-network experts (OSINT researchers, journalists, fact-checkers and academics) from across Europe. During the 2024 EU elections the network produced dozens of alerts sent to EU institutions, government agencies, platforms and advocacy groups. Alliance4Europe builds shared infrastructure such as TRANSCRIPT (a threat-intelligence and coordination platform) and a Disruption Toolkit, and it documents AI-enabled tactics including AI-generated imagery, impersonation of credible institutions and coordinated inauthentic behavior, for example unlabelled AI-generated images in political campaigns and AI-driven interference in Germany's 2025 federal election.
aiDemocracyAngle: Coordinates Europe's researchers and fact-checkers to detect and disrupt AI-generated disinformation and influence operations around elections.

name: Apart Research
tagline: Global research sprints, including on AI 'secret loyalties'
description: Apart Research is an independent AI-safety organization that runs global research sprints (hackathons), fellowships and mentorship to broaden participation in AI safety, including across the Global South. Several of its sprints target power-relevant threats directly, notably a 2026 'Secret Loyalties' hackathon investigating AI systems covertly trained to serve hidden controllers, a mechanism central to AI-enabled coup and disempowerment scenarios. Apart converts sprint outputs into peer-reviewed publications and has produced 40+ papers with 5,000+ sprint participants across dozens of nationalities. By decentralizing who gets to do AI-safety research, it also pushes back on the geographic and institutional concentration of AI-safety expertise itself. Its work spans model evaluation, multi-agent systems, interpretability and security, with some programs supported by Schmidt Sciences.
aiDemocracyAngle: Runs hands-on sprints on power-concentration mechanisms like 'secret loyalties,' and widens who can do safety research so expertise itself is less concentrated.

name: Apolitical
tagline: Global learning network upskilling public servants in AI and digital government
description: Apolitical, founded in 2015 by Robyn Scott and Lisa Witter, is a global peer-to-peer learning platform and social network for public servants, used by governments across more than 170 countries to share policy ideas, courses, and expertise and reduce duplicated effort. It offers online learning on government skills including a growing catalog of AI and digital-government training, connecting civil servants with experts, case studies, and each other. A mission-driven company (not a nonprofit), it has raised around 10 million pounds, including a Series A led by Systemiq Capital and Perivoli Innovations, and has been supported by an EU Horizon 2020 innovation grant. Apolitical's scale inside the public sector makes it an important channel for building the digital and AI capacity of democratic governments and for spreading institutional innovation between them.
aiDemocracyAngle: Apolitical is a mass distribution channel for AI and digital skills to civil servants worldwide, directly raising the capacity of democratic institutions to adopt technology.

name: Aspen Digital — AI Elections Initiative
tagline: Strengthening US election resilience against generative AI
description: The AI Elections Initiative is a program of Aspen Digital, part of the nonpartisan Aspen Institute, launched in 2024 to help the United States prepare for the first elections shaped by generative AI. Through convenings, briefings and practical resources it connects election officials, technology companies, media, national-security experts and civil society so they share threat information and effective solutions. It highlighted risks including hyperlocal voter suppression, multilingual influence operations and deepfakes, and produced guidance for administrators and journalists. The initiative is guided by an AI Elections Advisory Council co-chaired by Klon Kitchen, Alondra Nelson and former US election official Kim Wyman, and led by Vivian Schiller and Josh Lawson.
aiDemocracyAngle: Coordinates the people who run elections, build AI and cover politics so generative-AI election threats are met with shared, practical safeguards.

name: Ballotpedia
tagline: Nonpartisan encyclopedia of US politics; a grounding source for AI hubs
description: Ballotpedia is a nonpartisan online political encyclopedia founded in 2007 and published by the non-profit Lucy Burns Institute (Middleton, Wisconsin), led by founder and CEO Leslie Graves. Written and edited by a paid professional staff of dozens, it documents federal, state and local US politics (elections, candidates, officeholders, ballot measures and public policy), with a strong emphasis on the down-ballot and local races that other outlets neglect. It functions as a reference layer for voters, journalists and researchers rather than a matching tool. Perplexity chose Ballotpedia as one of the vetted, nonpartisan sources feeding its 2024 AI Election Information Hub, making it a de facto grounding source for AI election answers. It is an encyclopedia, not a VAA or AI product.
aiDemocracyAngle: A nonpartisan encyclopedic source AI systems (e.g. Perplexity's 2024 hub) draw on to ground election answers: infrastructure beneath AI voter tools.

name: BallotReady
tagline: US full-ballot voter guide with side-by-side down-ballot candidate research
description: BallotReady is a US civic-tech platform founded in 2015 by Alex Niemczewski and Aviva Rosman to help voters navigate the full ballot, down to obscure local races. Users enter their address and get their exact ballot with side-by-side candidate comparisons covering positions, experience, education, endorsements and biographical detail, then can save or print selections for the voting booth. A dedicated research team compiles nonpartisan data on candidates and offices nationwide (including judges, county commissions and school boards), drawn directly from local election offices. Through its organisations arm it also powers voter-engagement campaigns and an elections data API, aiming to reach tens of millions of voters across all 50 states. It is a research-driven voter-information tool rather than a questionnaire VAA or AI system.
aiDemocracyAngle: Down-ballot voter-information infrastructure whose nonpartisan candidate database is a data backbone others (including AI tools) can build on.

name: Berkman Klein Center — Applied Social Media Lab
tagline: Harvard center rebuilding the social internet to serve the public good
description: The Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society at Harvard University is a leading academic center studying the internet's impact on society, spanning platform governance, AI, privacy, and democracy. Within it, the Applied Social Media Lab (ASML), launched in 2024 as an offshoot of the Institute for Rebooting Social Media and funded by an eight-figure donation from Frank McCourt's Project Liberty, is an applied engineering lab where technologists and practitioners rebuild social-internet technology to serve the public good, free from commercial incentives. ASML builds tools focused on transparency and user control, healthier discourse, interoperability, and safety, including its open-source 'Frankly' discussion platform. While the Center's remit is broader than deliberative democracy, its work on discourse-quality technology, platform governance, and public-interest engineering directly overlaps with the AI-augmented collective-intelligence agenda.
aiDemocracyAngle: ASML engineers public-interest social technology for healthier discourse and user agency, applying AI and platform design to strengthen democratic communication.

name: Bertelsmann Stiftung — Upgrade Democracy
tagline: German foundation project countering disinformation and generative-AI manipulation
description: Upgrade Democracy is a project of the Bertelsmann Stiftung, one of Germany's largest foundations (established 1977). The project builds bridges between international actors to spread solutions that counter disinformation and that use digital tools to strengthen democracy, focusing on platform governance and the impact of AI on public opinion formation. It examines how generative AI enables synthetic, hyper-personalized information and disinformation, and commissioned a six-part international research series ('Countering Disinformation, Strengthening Democracy') between 2023 and 2024. Its outputs include the report 'Time to Act: Countering Disinformation for Stronger Democracies' and a Berlin conference convening ~130 experts from 25 countries.
aiDemocracyAngle: Upgrade Democracy studies how generative AI supercharges disinformation and platform manipulation, curating global countermeasures and pro-democracy digital tools.

name: Brennan Center for Justice — AI and Elections
tagline: Legal and policy safeguards against AI threats to elections
description: The Brennan Center for Justice at NYU School of Law is a nonpartisan law and policy institute (founded 1995) that works to strengthen democracy, including voting rights and election security. Its AI and Elections program analyzes how generative AI threatens free and fair elections, from deepfakes, AI-generated fake news sites and voice-cloning robocalls (like the 2024 fake Biden call in New Hampshire) to attacks on election officials and AI-backed voter suppression, and recommends concrete safeguards. The Center publishes research reports such as Artificial Intelligence and Election Security, Preparing to Fight AI-Backed Voter Suppression and guidance on detecting deceptive AI-generated election information, and it advocates for legislation mandating transparency and disclosure of AI in political communications. Combining litigation, research and policy advocacy, the Brennan Center is a leading US institutional voice translating AI-election risks into actionable law and administrative practice.
aiDemocracyAngle: Turns emerging AI-election threats (deepfakes, voice-cloning, voter suppression) into concrete legal safeguards and guidance for officials and lawmakers.

name: Burnes Center for Social Change / InnovateUS
tagline: Training public servants in responsible AI via InnovateUS, at scale
description: The Burnes Center for Social Change at Northeastern University, directed by Beth Simone Noveck, designs and implements practical, participatory, technology-enabled solutions to hard public problems; it is the institutional home of The GovLab and the InnovateUS training program. InnovateUS delivers free, evidence-based, at-your-own-pace courses and live workshops teaching public servants AI, data, digital, and innovation skills, reaching learners in 80 countries and across the U.S.; it received $5 million from Google.org, part of a $15 million Google.org pledge to train U.S. government staff in responsible AI. The Center also runs the AI for Impact Co-op Program, where students build AI for social good, and produces the Reboot Democracy blog and research. Together these make the Burnes Center one of the largest engines for building responsible-AI capacity inside democratic government, complementing the GovLab's research with hands-on public-sector upskilling at scale.
aiDemocracyAngle: InnovateUS is one of the largest efforts to teach public servants to use AI responsibly, directly raising the AI capacity of democratic institutions rather than just studying it.

name: Carnegie Endowment for International Peace
tagline: Democracy program plus the Information Environment Project on influence operations and AI
description: Founded in 1910, Carnegie is a leading global think tank whose Democracy, Conflict, and Governance Program studies democratic resilience. Its technology workstream centers on the Information Environment Project, which grew out of the Partnership for Countering Influence Operations (PCIO), a multi-year effort that built evidence-based measurement of influence operations, convened 40+ researchers with Princeton's Empirical Studies of Conflict Project, and founded the Influence Operations Researchers' Guild. Carnegie's Technology and International Affairs Program produces AI-and-democracy analysis, including 'AI Agents and Democratic Resilience' (2025) and 'AI and Democracy: Mapping the Intersections' (2026), examining how generative AI reshapes elections, disinformation, and governance.
aiDemocracyAngle: The Information Environment Project and PCIO build rigorous measurement of AI-enabled influence operations, while Carnegie's tech program maps how AI agents affect democratic resilience.

name: Center for AI and Digital Policy (CAIDP)
tagline: AI governance grounded in democratic values and the rule of law
description: The Center for AI and Digital Policy (CAIDP) is an independent nonprofit based in Washington, DC, established in 2021 and led by former EPIC president Marc Rotenberg. Its mission is to promote a fairer, more just society in which technology serves fundamental rights, democratic institutions and the rule of law. CAIDP assesses national AI policies, trains AI policy leaders through a global cohort program, and provides expert advice to governments and international bodies such as the OECD, UNESCO, Council of Europe and G7. Its flagship publication, the annual AI and Democratic Values Index, is a comparative study rating countries' AI policies and practices against democratic-governance metrics. CAIDP also files public comments and complaints, including an FTC complaint over generative AI, pushing for enforceable safeguards, transparency and accountability in AI deployment worldwide.
aiDemocracyAngle: Benchmarks and pressures governments to align AI policy with democratic values, rights and the rule of law via its AI and Democratic Values Index.

name: Center for an Informed Public (University of Washington)
tagline: UW research center on misinformation; co-led the Election Integrity Partnership
description: The Center for an Informed Public (CIP), founded in 2019 at the University of Washington with Knight and Hewlett Foundation funding, is an interdisciplinary research center that studies misinformation and works to resist strategic manipulation, promote an informed society, and strengthen democratic discourse. Led by researchers including Kate Starbird, it is known for rapid-response research on election rumors and collective sensemaking during crises, using computational methods to analyze how false claims spread on social platforms (e.g., its ElectionRumors datasets). CIP co-founded the Election Integrity Partnership with the Stanford Internet Observatory to track election misinformation in 2020 and 2022, and continues election-rumor research after that partnership wound down in 2024.
aiDemocracyAngle: CIP applies computational analysis to how election rumors and AI-amplified misinformation spread online, providing the research base for platform and policy responses that protect democratic discourse.
funders: John S. and James L. Knight Foundation

name: Center for Democracy & Technology (CDT)
tagline: Digital-rights group with an AI Governance Lab and an Elections & Democracy team
description: CDT (founded 1994) is a Washington- and Brussels-based nonprofit championing civil liberties and democracy in the digital age. It launched the AI Governance Lab in May 2023, led by Miranda Bogen and Kevin Bankston, to develop technically informed solutions for regulating and governing AI systems. Its Elections & Democracy team conducts real-time research on how AI affects elections, from campaign uses and deepfakes to whether widely used AI chatbots return accurate voting information; in one report with Proof News, CDT showed five major chatbots gave misleading answers about voting accessibility for people with disabilities. CDT also publishes 'Election Integrity Recommendations for Generative AI Developers.'
aiDemocracyAngle: CDT pairs its AI Governance Lab with an Elections & Democracy program to test AI systems for election harms and set integrity standards for generative-AI developers.

name: Center on Long-Term Risk
tagline: Cooperative AI research to prevent catastrophic conflict between AI systems
description: The Center on Long-Term Risk (CLR) is a London-based research and grantmaking nonprofit focused on worst-case ('s-risk') outcomes from advanced AI, with a major line of work on cooperative AI. Its cooperative-AI agenda studies how to prevent catastrophic cooperation failures between advanced AI systems, through research on credible commitments, bargaining, and Safe Pareto Improvements, alongside work on AI 'propensities,' model personas, and misuse. Programs include the Safe Pareto Improvements research agenda and fundamentals program, a Model Persona research agenda, a Summer Research Fellowship, a Research Affiliates program, and the CLR Fund for grantmaking. Originally founded as the Foundational Research Institute around 2013 and later rebranded, CLR is a registered charity in England and Wales. Its cooperative-AI work overlaps with the multi-agent-safety questions that determine whether AI systems deployed by many actors can coordinate without conflict.
aiDemocracyAngle: CLR's cooperative-AI research on bargaining and commitments among AI agents is foundational to whether multi-agent, multi-institution AI ecosystems cooperate rather than escalate conflict.

name: Centre for International Governance Innovation (CIGI)
tagline: Mainstream think tank on AI, power balance and democracy
description: The Centre for International Governance Innovation (CIGI) is an independent, non-partisan think tank based in Waterloo, Canada, founded in 2001, whose research spans data, transformative technology, security and democracy. Its AI work explicitly examines the concentration of AI innovation and power: publications analyze how AI and frontier labs can shift the balance of power among peoples and nations, and argue for checks and balances to limit the concentration of power AI enables. CIGI's 2025–2030 strategic plan foregrounds AI and transformative technology; data, economy and society; digitalization, security and democracy; and global cooperation. Compared with newer AI-safety labs, CIGI brings a mainstream international-relations and public-policy lens, publishing peer-reviewed research, foresight and policy commentary aimed at governments and multilateral bodies grappling with AI's implications for democratic governance and the global order.
aiDemocracyAngle: Brings mainstream international-governance analysis to AI power concentration, arguing for checks and balances on how AI shifts power among citizens, firms and states.

name: Centre for the Governance of AI (GovAI)
tagline: Scholarly hub for frontier-AI governance and institutional power questions
description: The Centre for the Governance of AI (GovAI) is an independent research organization (spun out of Oxford's Future of Humanity Institute, now a US 501(c)(3) with a UK arm) that produces scholarship and trains talent to help decision-makers navigate advanced AI. Its research spans technical AI governance, the economics of AI-driven labor displacement, threat modeling of dual-use capabilities, and the governance of AI agents. Several of these strands bear on how power could concentrate as AI diffuses through the economy and state. GovAI researchers have contributed foundational work on questions like preventing dangerous concentrations of AI capability, corporate governance of frontier labs, and windfall/benefit-sharing mechanisms. Its analysis is regularly cited by MIT Technology Review, The Economist, Foreign Affairs and the New York Times. GovAI functions as a scholarly hub connecting academics, labs and policymakers on the structural and institutional risks of transformative AI.
aiDemocracyAngle: A scholarly hub for governance research on frontier-lab power, labor displacement and agent infrastructure: the institutional levers that decide whether AI concentrates power.

name: CETaS — Centre for Emerging Technology and Security
tagline: UK research on AI threats to elections and national security
description: The Centre for Emerging Technology and Security (CETaS) is the UK's national research centre on emerging technology and security, based at the Alan Turing Institute (the UK's national institute for data science and AI) and launched in 2022. Since early 2024 it has produced a leading evidence base on AI's impact on elections and democracy. Its three 2024 reports (a briefing surveying AI threats across 19 elections, an analysis of AI-enabled influence operations in the 2024 UK, EU and French elections, and Safeguarding Future Elections) found little conclusive evidence that AI-generated disinformation changed 2024 results, while warning of real risks to trust and information integrity. CETaS calls for measures such as mandated platform data access for researchers and stronger deterrents against creating and sharing disinformation. It bridges rigorous empirical analysis with actionable recommendations for UK security and electoral institutions.
aiDemocracyAngle: Provides the UK's most rigorous evidence base on how AI-enabled influence operations affect elections, and what safeguards actually work.

name: Code for America
tagline: Making government services work through the mindful use of technology and AI
description: Code for America is a nonpartisan 501(c)(3), founded in 2009, that works with government and communities to make public services simple, accessible, and effective through the mindful use of technology. Its programs span the social safety net (simplifying access to SNAP, Medicaid, and tax benefits), criminal-justice record clearance, and, increasingly, artificial intelligence. It recently launched a Government AI Landscape Assessment evaluating state-level AI readiness and formed a partnership with Anthropic to help governments adopt AI responsibly in service delivery. Code for America also runs a national Summit, FormFest, and a Work Requirements Implementation Toolkit, and holds a four-star Charity Navigator rating. Its core is service delivery rather than deliberation, but its AI-in-government work shapes whether AI strengthens or degrades the everyday functioning of democratic institutions.
aiDemocracyAngle: Code for America shapes how AI enters frontline government service delivery, a decisive but under-discussed channel through which AI affects citizens' lived experience of democratic institutions.

name: Coefficient Giving
tagline: Formerly Open Philanthropy: the largest global funder of AI safety
description: Coefficient Giving, rebranded from Open Philanthropy in November 2025, is widely considered the largest funder of AI safety and governance globally. Since 2014 it has directed roughly $336M (about 12% of total grants) to AI safety research and governance, including around $46M in 2023 alone. The rebrand reflects a shift from serving primarily one anchor donor, Good Ventures (the foundation of Dustin Moskovitz and Cari Tuna), to operating 13 cause-specific pooled funds open to multiple philanthropists; in 2025 more than $200M in commitments came from other funders, with new backers including Stripe's Patrick Collison, Lucy Southworth, and Bill Gates. Its AI governance and policy grantmaking funds work on frontier-model safety, compute governance, and the concentration of power that advanced AI could enable, supporting think tanks, technical labs, and policy organizations. While not framed primarily as democracy funding, its power-concentration and governance work directly bears on preserving democratic control over transformative AI.
aiDemocracyAngle: As the largest AI-safety and AI-governance funder, its grants on frontier-AI policy and power concentration directly shape whether democratic institutions retain control over transformative AI.

name: Collective Intelligence Project (CIP)
tagline: Steering transformative AI toward better outcomes, for everyone
description: The Collective Intelligence Project (CIP) is a nonprofit R&D lab co-founded in 2023 by Divya Siddarth and Saffron Huang to build democratic and participatory mechanisms for governing transformative technologies, especially AI. CIP designs collective-intelligence processes that channel broad public input into AI development and evaluation. With Anthropic it created Collective Constitutional AI, running a Polis deliberation with ~1,000 Americans to draft a public constitution used to fine-tune a language model, one of the first times the public collectively directed a model's behavior. Other projects include Global Dialogues (structured deliberations with thousands worldwide), Weval (an open platform for community-built AI evaluations), Alignment Assemblies and Community Models. CIP publishes a Roadmap for Democratic AI. Funders listed on its site include Omidyar Network, the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, the Survival and Flourishing Fund, Google.org and Fast Forward.
aiDemocracyAngle: Builds and tests real mechanisms for the public to collectively shape how AI systems behave and are governed.

name: Computational Democracy Project (Pol.is)
tagline: Open-source ML platform surfacing consensus in large-scale online deliberation
description: The Computational Democracy Project is a nonprofit that stewards Pol.is, an open-source platform for large-scale online deliberation launched in 2012 by Colin Megill, Christopher Small, and Michael Bjorkegren. Participants submit short statements and vote agree/disagree on others' statements; there are no replies, which reduces trolling. Machine-learning dimensionality reduction and clustering then map participants into opinion groups in real time and, crucially, elevate statements that find consensus across otherwise divided clusters. The nonprofit was formed in 2018 to sustain the open-source code and mission. Pol.is is the technical backbone of vTaiwan and has hosted tens of thousands of conversations reaching millions of participants worldwide. The project actively researches how large language models can extend deliberation: summarizing arguments, generating candidate consensus statements, and scaling facilitation. That makes it a bridge between classic civic tech and AI-augmented collective intelligence.
aiDemocracyAngle: Pol.is pioneered ML-driven consensus discovery and now researches LLM-assisted deliberation, a foundational reference design for AI-augmented collective decision-making.

name: Consul Democracy
tagline: Open-source e-participation software deployed by 250+ cities and organizations
description: Consul Democracy is a free, open-source e-participation and open-government platform, originally built as Decide Madrid and launched by Madrid City Council in September 2015. It lets citizens submit proposals, debate, vote on new policies, and run participatory budgeting and public consultations, giving residents a direct channel into local decision-making. Built in Ruby on Rails with PostgreSQL and Elasticsearch and licensed under AGPL, the software has been adopted by more than 250 cities and organizations worldwide, gaining especially strong traction across Latin America and Europe. Governance of the project moved from the City of Madrid to an independent nonprofit stewarding the open-source codebase and community. Like Decidim, Consul is core participation infrastructure rather than an AI tool per se, but it is a widely deployed platform layer on which AI-assisted analysis of citizen proposals and deliberation can be built.
aiDemocracyAngle: Consul is globally deployed participation infrastructure whose large citizen-proposal datasets are natural targets for AI analysis and sensemaking layers.

name: Convergence Analysis
tagline: Scenario and governance research on AI's structural and race risks
description: Convergence Analysis is a nonprofit AI-governance research organization that models plausible AI futures and designs policy interventions to steer away from catastrophic outcomes. Its three tracks (scenario research, governance research and AI awareness) include work directly relevant to power concentration, such as 'The Manhattan Trap,' which analyzes the destabilizing race dynamics of a national superintelligence project, plus studies of AI's economic disruption (its Threshold 2030 conference) and global governance strategies. Convergence develops concrete governance mechanisms, such as chip and model registries and monitoring frameworks, intended to distribute oversight and prevent unchecked concentration of AI capability. It contributes to reference works like the Oxford Handbook of AI Governance and runs fellowships producing analysis on workforce impacts, US–China dynamics and public AI funding. The organization publishes research and policy recommendations aimed at the AI-safety and policymaking communities.
aiDemocracyAngle: Scenario and governance research on how superintelligence races and economic shocks could concentrate power, plus institutional mechanisms to keep oversight distributed.

name: Cooperative AI Foundation
tagline: Building the field of cooperative AI so multi-agent systems can safely coordinate
description: The Cooperative AI Foundation (CAIF) is a UK-registered charity that builds the research field of cooperative AI: ensuring that AI agents deployed by many different actors can coordinate, bargain, and avoid catastrophic cooperation failures. It funds and convenes work on multi-agent safety, behavioral mechanism design, democratic oversight of AI, and open-source game theory. In 2025 it launched a $10 million Multi-Agent Safety Fund together with Schmidt Sciences, Google DeepMind, and ARIA, and it runs an annual PhD Fellowship (14 fellows in the 2026 cohort), a summer school, a monthly seminar series, and an open 'Introduction to Cooperative AI' curriculum. Its board includes Google DeepMind's Thore Graepel and Taiwan's former Digital Minister Audrey Tang, tying the foundation directly to digital-democracy practice. CAIF made its first major grant to CMU's FOCAL lab.
aiDemocracyAngle: Cooperative AI is the substrate for collective and institutional decision-making: if multiple AI agents cannot cooperate safely, neither can the institutions that deploy them. CAIF explicitly funds democratic-oversight and multi-actor coordination research.

name: CORDA
tagline: Non-profit building open-source tool & research for democracy in the age of AI
description: CORDA is a non-profit, open-source organization with the mission to research, build and scale the future of democracy. Its flagship program, the CORDA Democracy Fellowship, runs recurring part-time remote cohorts of about eight weeks (inaugural cohort Spring 2026, roughly 8-10 hours per week). Fellows from research, engineering, product, design, policy, law and communications advance concrete projects with mentorship, clustered around themes like democratic health, collective reasoning and deliberation, election-information tooling, and AI governance. The fellowship is unpaid, awards prizes for outstanding projects, and aims at deployable tools rather than pure academic research. CORDA also maintains this map.
aiDemocracyAngle: Channels part-time talent into deployable AI-for-democracy tools and maintains this ecosystem map. Concentrates effort on a neglected, high-leverage space: using AI to strengthen elections, deliberation, and democratic institutions.

name: Cortico
tagline: Nonprofit AI platform surfacing unheard community voices at scale
description: Cortico is a nonprofit co-founded by Deb Roy that builds and operates the Local Voices Network (LVN), a conversation platform using AI to surface underheard perspectives and foster constructive public dialogue across political and cultural divides. Small groups hold facilitated, recorded conversations; Cortico then combines human-led and AI-assisted 'sensemaking' to identify patterns, themes, and insights across many conversations, connecting them into a network of community engagement. The platform is positioned as an alternative to engagement-optimized social media, aiming to illuminate the nuance of individual perspectives and give civic institutions, journalists, and community organizations a way to listen at scale. Cortico works closely with the MIT Center for Constructive Communication, which supplies research methods and models, while Cortico handles real-world deployment with communities. Together they treat AI as a listening and bridging tool rather than a broadcast amplifier.
aiDemocracyAngle: Cortico applies AI sensemaking to facilitated community conversations, turning dispersed lived experience into structured input for civic decision-makers.

name: Cosmos Institute
tagline: Funds AI research and prototypes for a free society and human autonomy
description: The Cosmos Institute is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit dedicated to human flourishing in the age of AI, building on three pillars it names reason, decentralization, and human autonomy, drawing on Mill, Tocqueville, and Aristotle. It funds and conducts research at the intersection of philosophy and AI, and backs founders and researchers building institutions that help people author their own lives and renew free society. Its Cosmos Grants provide fast, small-scale funding ($1,000-$10,000) for early-stage AI prototypes that strengthen human capacities, each expected to ship a major deliverable within three months. It also runs fellowships placing scholars at partner labs and supported a Human-Centered AI Lab at the University of Oxford focused on flourishing principles in open-source AI. With FIRE it launched a $1M grant program for AI that advances truth-seeking and free expression. Founding fellows include Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark, signaling close ties to the frontier AI community.
aiDemocracyAngle: Explicitly frames its grantmaking around decentralization, human autonomy, and free society, funding AI tools that resist concentration and strengthen open discourse and truth-seeking.

name: Council on Technology and Social Cohesion
tagline: Uniting technologists and peacebuilders around prosocial, cohesion-first design
description: The Council on Technology and Social Cohesion is a field-catalyzing initiative that brings together technologists and peacebuilders to design technology that protects human dignity, strengthens social bonds, and supports collaborative problem-solving. Emerging from a 2020 working group and convened by peacebuilding organizations, including Search for Common Ground, the Toda Peace Institute, Braver Angels, More in Common, and the Alliance for Peacebuilding, it focuses on 'tech for social cohesion' as complementary to, but distinct from, work on disinformation, privacy, and trust-and-safety. It prioritizes conflict-affected communities and preventing online harms from triggering real-world violence. Its work includes prosocial-design resources and, with the Plurality Institute and Prosocial Design Network, an 'LLM Map' cataloging tools that use language models for public discourse. The Council aims to make prosocial, cohesion-strengthening technology desirable, affordable, and actionable, treating platform and AI design as a lever for democratic resilience and peace.
aiDemocracyAngle: The Council reframes platform and AI design around social cohesion and peacebuilding, directly connecting how recommender systems and LLM tools are built to whether democracies fracture or hold together.

name: Data & Society
tagline: Studying AI's social impact and building democratic power over tech
description: Data & Society Research Institute is an independent nonprofit founded in 2014 by danah boyd that studies the social, ethical and political implications of data-centric and automated technologies. Its research programs, including AI on the Ground, Labor Futures and Trustworthy Infrastructure, analyze how AI systems shape society and governance. Its democracy work centers on public participation and civic power: it has convened events and published primers such as Enrolling Citizens: A Primer on Archetypes of Democratic Engagement with AI and Democratizing AI: Principles for Meaningful Public Participation, and hosted discussions on rewiring democracy in the age of AI. In 2026 it launched AI Civics, a public-education program backed by $2 million from the Humanity AI funder collaborative, to strengthen channels for the public to shape how AI is designed and deployed. Data & Society is an influential source of critical, empirical scholarship on AI and society.
aiDemocracyAngle: Produces empirical research and public-education programs to give citizens real influence over how AI is designed, deployed and governed.

name: Decidim
tagline: Open-source participatory-democracy framework used by cities worldwide
description: Decidim (Catalan for 'we decide') is a free, open-source digital platform for participatory democracy, first released around 2016–2017 by Barcelona City Council and now maintained by the international Metadecidim community under an AGPL license. Built in Ruby on Rails, it lets any organization (city councils, regions, universities, NGOs, cooperatives) run participatory processes such as strategic planning, participatory budgeting, public consultations, collaborative regulation drafting, and assemblies, with strong emphasis on transparency, traceability, and democratic guarantees. Decidim has been adopted by cities and institutions worldwide, including Barcelona, Helsinki, Mexico City, and regions such as Québec and Puglia. As mature, self-hostable civic infrastructure it is a backbone for online participation across Europe and Latin America. While its core is pre-AI participation tooling, Decidim increasingly explores integrations for summarizing and analyzing citizen input, and is a key platform layer the AI-deliberation ecosystem builds upon.
aiDemocracyAngle: Decidim is the dominant open-source participation backbone that AI sensemaking tools plug into, making it critical infrastructure for tech-augmented democracy.

name: Democracy Technologies
tagline: Independent magazine and database mapping the democracy-tech field
description: Democracy Technologies is an independent online magazine and resource dedicated to digital tools that strengthen democracy. A project of the Innovation in Politics Institute, it provides people working in politics and the democracy-technology industry with in-depth coverage of new developments in digital participation, deliberation, e-voting, AI and data, and other civic tools. Alongside articles, interviews, 'getting started' guides, and opinion pieces, it maintains an independently curated, filterable database of digital tools for citizen participation, i-voting, and political-party organizing, searchable by region, software type, data functionality, and communication features. As a media and knowledge-infrastructure organization rather than a tool-builder or research lab, Democracy Technologies helps practitioners track and compare platforms, including AI-augmented deliberation tools, and its editorial coverage regularly examines how AI is reshaping participation, deliberation, and governance.
aiDemocracyAngle: It tracks and explains the AI-and-democracy tooling landscape for practitioners, serving as a mapping and comparison hub across the ecosystem.

name: Democracy Works / TurboVote
tagline: Nonpartisan US voter-turnout tech; its data grounded Perplexity's 2024 AI hub
description: Democracy Works is a nonpartisan US non-profit founded in 2010 that builds technology to make voting easier. Its flagship, TurboVote, helps citizens register to vote, request absentee ballots, find polling places, and receive election reminders, and it partners with hundreds of colleges, companies and non-profits; its Elections API and voter tools reach millions each cycle. In 2022 it supported more than 1,500 elections and sent over 54 million election notifications. In 2024 Democracy Works supplied authoritative election data (alongside the Associated Press) to power Perplexity's AI Election Information Hub, positioning its verified data as a trusted grounding source for AI systems. Democracy Works is civic infrastructure rather than a VAA, and a bridge between nonpartisan election data and AI tools.
aiDemocracyAngle: Its verified election data grounded Perplexity's 2024 AI Election Hub: a concrete example of nonpartisan data feeding LLM voter tools.

name: DemocracyNext
tagline: International institute scaling permanent, empowered citizens' assemblies
description: DemocracyNext is an international, non-partisan research and action institute founded in 2022 by Claudia Chwalisz, who previously established and led the OECD's work on innovative citizen participation. Its mission is to scale high-quality, empowered, and permanent citizens' assemblies, deliberative bodies built on three principles: sortition (random selection of members), deliberation (structured, informed discussion), and rotation (regularly changing who holds decision-making power). The institute researches and designs new democratic institutions, publishes guidance and standards, and works with governments and civil society to embed assemblies into how public decisions are made across domains such as urban planning, technology, and climate. DemocracyNext also examines how deliberative democracy intersects with emerging technology and AI governance, and how assemblies could give citizens real power over consequential decisions. It is a leading global convener and standard-setter for the deliberative-democracy movement.
aiDemocracyAngle: DemocracyNext promotes citizens' assemblies as the venue for governing AI and technology, and studies how deliberative bodies can steer consequential tech decisions.

name: Demos / CASM (Demos Digital)
tagline: UK think tank researching AI, social media and democracy
description: Demos is Britain's leading cross-party think tank (founded 1993). In 2012 it established the Centre for the Analysis of Social Media (CASM), the first UK think-tank unit dedicated to studying how the digital world affects politics and policy; it now operates as Demos Digital, the organization's digital-policy hub, under a Trustworthy Technology pillar. Co-founded by Carl Miller, the unit blends data science with social research to examine online discourse, disinformation and the governance of AI. Recent work includes the 2026 Electoral Hallucinations report on safeguarding UK elections in a world of large language models and AI chatbots, research on generative AI's effects on elections and democracy, and projects on democratizing technology development and putting the public at the heart of AI-governance decisions. Demos combines rigorous research with concrete policy recommendations to UK government and regulators.
aiDemocracyAngle: Researches how chatbots, recommender systems and generative AI affect UK elections and public debate, and how to govern them democratically.

name: DGAP AI/Democracy Initiative
tagline: Evidence-based research on AI's role in elections and democratic resilience
description: The AI/Democracy Initiative sits within the Center for Geopolitics, Geoeconomics, and Technology at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP), Germany's leading foreign-policy think tank. Run in collaboration with the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, it applies quantitative and qualitative research to real elections (the 2024 votes in Mexico, South Africa, India and the United States, the European Parliament elections, and German state elections in Brandenburg, Saxony and Thuringia) to map vulnerabilities related to AI and identify trends in electoral processes. Its goal is to convert findings into evidence-based best practices for more resilient democracies, informing responses to the 2025 German federal election and beyond. Related DGAP work (Mapping Democracy Towards AI-Strengthened Political Discourse) explores how AI could strengthen, not just threaten, political discourse. The initiative combines rigorous election-monitoring data with policy recommendations for European and German decision-makers.
aiDemocracyAngle: Studies how AI shaped real 2024–25 elections across continents to produce evidence-based safeguards for democratic resilience.

name: Digital Forensic Research Lab (DFRLab), Atlantic Council
tagline: OSINT lab exposing influence operations; runs the Democracy + Tech Initiative
description: The DFRLab, incubated at the Atlantic Council in 2016, combines technical and policy expertise on disinformation, connective technologies, democracy, and digital rights. It has conducted 1,000+ open-source (OSINT) investigations exposing influence operations, foreign interference, and emerging digital threats worldwide, and works to promote digital resilience and defend democratic institutions. Its Democracy + Tech Initiative develops policy practices that steer technology and governance toward open societies. DFRLab increasingly focuses on AI: its training academies equip participants to identify and counter AI-enabled surveillance, manipulation, and harassment, and its research tracks AI-generated content in influence operations.
aiDemocracyAngle: DFRLab's OSINT investigations and Democracy + Tech Initiative expose AI-enabled influence operations and surveillance, building digital resilience for democracies.

name: Effective Institutions Project
tagline: Helping donors improve the institutions that will govern transformative AI
description: The Effective Institutions Project (EIP) is a research and philanthropic-advising organization that helps donors and decision-makers improve the world's most consequential institutions during what it calls 'The Decisive Decade.' It focuses on four domains: governance of transformative AI, institutional resilience and accountability, reducing risks from great-power conflict, and pandemic prevention. EIP analyzes which specific institutions (governments, companies, international bodies) most shape critical outcomes, then advises funders on high-leverage interventions and produces publications on institutional decision-making and AI governance. It positions institutional quality (how key organizations make and implement decisions) as an underrated lever on catastrophic and systemic risk. EIP maintains a team, a publications library, and a careers/get-involved pipeline, and is active on the AI-governance side of the effective-altruism and institutional-reform communities.
aiDemocracyAngle: EIP treats 'governance of transformative AI' and institutional decision quality as one problem: improving how the institutions that will wield AI actually decide.

name: ElectOMate
tagline: Open-source non-profit AI voting assistant, a 'Perplexity for politics'
description: ElectOMate is a non-profit, open-source AI voting-advice platform run by OpenDemocracy. It combines a classic questionnaire with interactive AI chat and voice calls grounded in official party programmes, plus tailored web search and a prototype media-bias checker. Technically it is built on agentic AI pipelines and retrieval-augmented generation over hand-curated, official sources such as party manifestos and debate records, aiming to reduce bias and hallucination; it describes itself as 'Perplexity for politics' and collects no user data. It first launched around the 2024 European Parliament elections and works with governments and civic partners to cover elections worldwide, with links to ETH Zurich's Student Project House. It is closely tied to the CORDA Democracy Fellowship, which is also hosted by Open Democracy AI.
aiDemocracyAngle: An explicitly AI-native VAA using RAG and agentic pipelines over official manifestos to give grounded, source-cited voting guidance across many countries.

name: EU DisinfoLab
tagline: Independent European nonprofit tackling sophisticated disinformation
description: EU DisinfoLab is an independent Brussels-based nonprofit that investigates and counters disinformation targeting the EU, its member states and core democratic values. It conducts original investigations (notably exposing large cross-platform influence operations such as Doppelganger), publishes research and policy recommendations to EU institutions and member states, and maintains a European platform and expert community for collaboration among researchers and fact-checkers. Its AI Disinfo Hub is a dedicated resource on AI and disinformation, collecting Neural News, research reports, podcasts and tools for researchers, policymakers and the public, alongside a complementary AI against disinformation strand on defensive uses. EU DisinfoLab also runs the annual #Disinfo conference. It combines investigative rigor with EU-level advocacy for stronger platform accountability under frameworks like the Digital Services Act.
aiDemocracyAngle: Investigates and helps the field counter AI-accelerated disinformation campaigns aimed at European elections and democratic institutions.

name: euandi
tagline: Pan-European academic VAA from the EUI, 20+ languages, 290 parties
description: euandi (EU&I) is a pan-European voting advice application developed by the European University Institute (EUI) in Florence, using a non-partisan methodology first built in 2009 (predecessor: EU Profiler). For the 2024 European Parliament elections it was available in over 20 languages; an international team of more than 170 political scientists coded the positions of some 290 parties. Users answer a battery of policy statements and are matched to parties through a combination of party self-placement and expert judgement, then placed on a European political map. The 2024 edition was completed by about 850,000 users in its first 30 days. Its anonymised data is regularly released to researchers. It is a classic academic questionnaire VAA rather than an AI tool.
aiDemocracyAngle: The flagship academic, EU-wide classic VAA; its expert-coded, multilingual datasets are a major research resource on European party positioning.

name: Federation of American Scientists
tagline: Science-grounded policy building government capacity to govern AI
description: The Federation of American Scientists (FAS), founded in 1945 by Manhattan Project scientists, is a nonpartisan policy organization that brings scientific and technical rigor to public policy. Through its Day One Project, FAS crowdsources actionable, evidence-based policy ideas and incubates them into government action across priority areas including government capacity, R&D, global security, and emerging technologies and AI. Its AI-and-government-capacity work has proposed measures such as a federal center of excellence for state and local AI procurement, an 'AI Corps' embedding specialists across agencies, and detailed responses to national AI Action Plans. FAS pairs an in-house policy team with a wide network of technologists and scientists to place experts and ideas inside government. Its focus on state capacity and responsible technology adoption makes it a key actor in ensuring democratic governments can competently understand, procure, and govern AI.
aiDemocracyAngle: FAS works on the state-capacity side of AI and democracy: getting competent AI talent, procurement, and policy inside government so democratic institutions can govern the technology.

name: FIDE — Federation for Innovation in Democracy
tagline: Independent go-to body for designing and evaluating citizens' assemblies
description: FIDE (Federation for Innovation in Democracy) is an independent, non-partisan, non-profit federation that supports governments and practitioners in designing, running, and evaluating citizens' assemblies and other deliberative processes across Europe and North America. Founded to be the European 'go-to' organization for the deliberative field, filling a gap where appetite for democratic innovation outpaced available expertise, FIDE stewards a network of democratic innovators and provides evidence-based, non-commercial advice, design principles, standards, and practical guides on citizen participation, deliberative democracy, and civic lottery (sortition). Its experts have helped design landmark processes including the permanent 'Ostbelgien Model' (the first standing institution with citizens drafted by lot) and the Assemblée Citoyenne of Paris. FIDE convenes forums and festivals bringing the field together and works to safeguard the integrity, quality, and impact of deliberative processes as they move 'from novel to normal.' It is primarily a deliberative-democracy institution rather than an AI organization.
aiDemocracyAngle: FIDE sets quality standards for deliberative processes that AI facilitation and analysis tools must meet, shaping how technology is responsibly integrated into assemblies.

name: FOCAL @ CMU (Foundations of Cooperative AI Lab)
tagline: CMU lab rebuilding game theory so autonomous AI agents cooperate
description: The Foundations of Cooperative AI Lab (FOCAL) at Carnegie Mellon University, led by Professor Vincent Conitzer, works to rebuild the foundations of game theory so they fit advanced, autonomous AI agents, with the explicit goal of achieving cooperation. Research directions include designing preferences, beliefs and identities for AI; open-source game theory and multilateral commitments; foundations of multi-agent learning; decision-theoretic foundations for game theory; and self-locating beliefs. Conitzer also heads Technical AI Engagement at Oxford's Institute for Ethics in AI and teaches a graduate course, 'Foundations of Cooperative AI.' The lab is supported by a $3 million gift from the Center for Emerging Risk Research and a $500,000 gift from the Cooperative AI Foundation, whose first major grant it received. FOCAL is a central academic node in the cooperative-AI ecosystem, connecting technical game theory to AI alignment and social choice.
aiDemocracyAngle: FOCAL's work on social choice, commitments and multi-agent cooperation underpins how AI systems could aggregate preferences and support collective decision-making, core machinery for AI-mediated democratic institutions.

name: Ford Foundation (Technology and Society)
tagline: Anchored the $200M+ funder push for AI in the public interest
description: The Ford Foundation, one of the largest US foundations (endowed by the Ford motor fortune), runs a Technology and Society program that pioneered the field of public interest technology, ensuring communities historically harmed by technology are reflected in its development and governance. The program makes grants generally from $50,000 to $500,000 for advocacy, research, and organizing to advance public-interest technology policy and design grounded in justice and equity. Ford's Public Interest Technology Catalyst Fund committed a $50M grant budget in 2020 and helped mobilize more than $130M in complementary grantmaking. Most relevant to AI and democracy, Ford led and anchored a multi-funder initiative to ensure AI advances the public interest, with participating philanthropies pledging more than $200M to mitigate AI harms and promote responsible innovation, and it provided core support to organizations such as Reset Tech. Ford blends grantmaking with impact investing and field-building across civil society, academia, and government.
aiDemocracyAngle: Led the $200M+ cross-funder initiative to ensure AI advances the public interest and funds public-interest-technology work grounded in justice and democratic equity.

name: Foresight Institute
tagline: Champions decentralized 'd/acc' and AI-for-democracy futures
description: The Foresight Institute is a San Francisco nonprofit (founded 1986) that advances beneficial development of transformative technologies: nanotech, biotech, neurotech and AI. Through its Existential Hope program and AI-focused work, Foresight explores futures that avoid both catastrophe and authoritarian concentration of power, championing 'd/acc' (decentralized, democratic, defensive acceleration) and 'Tool AI' as alternatives to centralized, uncontrollable systems. It has run institution-design hackathons (with the Future of Life Institute) to prototype governance for transformative AI, published AI Pathways scenario reports, and convened events such as 'Supercooperation: The Future of AI for Democracy.' Foresight also supported early work connected to the Windfall Trust. By focusing on decentralization, cooperation and positive visions, it contributes design ideas and community for keeping AI's trajectory pluralistic and democratically accountable rather than concentrated.

name: Forethought Research
tagline: Superintelligence-transition research; authors of 'AI-Enabled Coups'
description: Forethought Research is a UK-registered nonprofit research organization studying how to navigate the transition to a world with superintelligent AI. Its fellows include Tom Davidson, William MacAskill and Mia Taylor. Forethought's most prominent contribution to the power-concentration literature is the 2025 report 'AI-Enabled Coups,' which argues that advanced AI could let a small group, or a single leader, seize and entrench control over powerful, even democratic, states by concentrating a vast, loyal AI workforce and, potentially, automated militaries whose 'secret loyalties' are hard to detect. The organization also researches intelligence-explosion dynamics, software-driven R&D acceleration, AI tools for existential security, and 'better futures' beyond mere catastrophe avoidance. Forethought publishes reports, a newsletter and the ForeCast podcast, positioning itself upstream of policy by clarifying strategic questions about how AI could reshape the distribution of power.
aiDemocracyAngle: Its 'AI-Enabled Coups' work is one of the most detailed treatments of how AI could let a tiny group seize a state, including via military AI with hidden loyalties.

keyProjects.name: AI-Enabled Coups
keyProjects.note: Tom Davidson et al. flagship report

name: Founders Pledge (Global Catastrophic Risks Fund)
tagline: Entrepreneur-backed fund covering AI risk and democratic resilience
description: Founders Pledge is a nonprofit that mobilizes charitable commitments from tech and business entrepreneurs and directs them to high-impact causes. Its Global Catastrophic Risks Fund (GCRF) targets far-future and large-scale threats, including risks from artificial intelligence, great-power war, nuclear war, and catastrophic biological risks. On AI, the fund has supported cross-democracy coordination, including a Track II dialogue convening experts from the US, Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan to inform AI policy on compute governance, export controls, and safety standards across Northeast Asian democracies, and a ~$300K grant coordinated with the Carnegie Endowment on decision-making around catastrophic risks of US-China AI competition. Other grantees include the Center for a New American Security, Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security, and INHR. Founders Pledge combines evidence-led research with pooled and advised funds, giving entrepreneurial donors a route into AI-safety and geopolitical-resilience work relevant to preserving democratic states' capacity to govern AI.
aiDemocracyAngle: Funds AI-safety coordination among allied democracies (US, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan) and US-China AI-competition risk work bearing on democratic states' ability to govern AI.
funders: Charitable pledges from tech and business entrepreneurs
